Firstly, on data.gouv.fr, anyone can publish data. It is an open and community-driven platform, allowing various stakeholders to contribute, including administrations, businesses, civil society, citizens, etc.

A discussion module is available for users for each dataset. They can express their opinion on the published dataset, whether it is positive or negative. This discussion module also makes it possible to report anomalies or areas for improvement to the producer.

We believe that this evaluation mechanism provides more qualitative information than a simple five-star mechanism. Indeed, a five-star mechanism does not provide information on the improvement prospects.  See example : [https://www.data.gouv.fr/fr/datasets/base-sirene-des-entreprises-et-de-leurs-etablissements-siren-siret/#/discussions](https://www.data.gouv.fr/fr/datasets/base-sirene-des-entreprises-et-de-leurs-etablissements-siren-siret/#/discussions)

Citizens can request data sets through two channels of communication :

- They can send a request at [ouverture@data.gouv.fr](mailto:ouverture@data.gouv.fr). Requests are handled by Etalab's team.
- They can send a request to the [CADA](https://www.cada.fr/) (commission of access to administrative documents). The commission is dedicated to receive open data requests in order to give administrative feedback.

Furthermore, we developed a tool to receive demands. The latter stands between an FAQ and a form. The main aim is to give generic answers to frenquently asked questions and get more qualified demands : [https://support.data.gouv.fr/](https://support.data.gouv.fr/)

column2:
Do you used the insights about portal usage and about the behaviour and needs of portal users to improve the portal accordingly?

For Explanation:
* If yes, please explain your process for improving the portal based on user insights and feedback
* If relevant, kindly highlight some improvements made in the past year
column4: new question
column7:
We apologize for the confusion.

Developments on data.gouv.fr are done in an agile manner and are primarily guided by:

1. User Feedback

The platform is primarily built based on user feedback, which comes from several sources:

- User tests and interviews
- Interviews serve to:
- Conduct forward-looking research and update the vision: maintaining a broad view of the users' context, their needs, sector evolution, and usage trends, rather than focusing solely on ongoing and planned work.
- Prepare for a future project that hasn't been tackled yet, to understand current usage, identify user problems, gather test data, and validate or invalidate proposed features.

- Tests serve to:
- Identify usability issues before coding, understand how the application is used, and detect its shortcomings.
- Test planned changes at a lower cost using more or less finished and interactive mockups before coding.
- Verify, once the changes are in production, whether they work "as expected".

Both approaches are essential for prioritizing upcoming work, limiting the influence of personal biases. Ideally, multiple elements or hypotheses are tested during a session with a user (as organizing it is time-consuming), and an "interview" part is included in the tests (with questions beyond what's on the screen).

- Support feedback
- Feedback received by the support team
The support team is in direct contact with users and regularly receives valuable feedback. However, it's important to note that this feedback mostly comes from data producers, who represent only a portion of our users and whose needs may sometimes conflict with those of data reusers.
- GitHub tickets
Some users, often advanced users or partners, propose improvements via GitHub.
- Feedback from social media and specialized platforms
Insights can often be gleaned from community discussions on platforms like teamopendata, Twitter, or LinkedIn. However, it's crucial to ensure the representativeness of this feedback compared to the rest of our users to avoid responding only to the loudest voices.

2. Usage Metrics

We monitor usage metrics, such as platform activity (views, downloads, data previews) and catalog evolution (data quality improvement, resource type evolution), to identify trends and ensure that our actions are heading in the right direction. However, we place greater importance on impact indicators (see below).

3. Team Feedback

The team is also a critical source for prioritization. While user feedback and usage should remain our guiding star, it's crucial to consider team feedback, especially for:

- Understanding the complexity and technical debt induced by developments
- Facilitating the work of the team (both the development team and the support team)
- Building a shared vision and ensuring team motivation

4. Other Types of Feedback

data.gouv.fr operates in a complex environment where feedback and directives can come from many sources (political mandates, ministries, management, European partners). This feedback must also be carefully considered and sometimes addressed strategically, even if it doesn't align perfectly with the product vision.

This working methodology does not prevent data.gouv.fr from having a roadmap.

The roadmap of data.gouv.fr serves as a guiding thread for the team and facilitates interactions with stakeholders. The team aims to be agile, so the roadmap is not set in stone and is not tied to specific dates or fixed deliverables.

Mission and Impact Objectives

Above all, the team pursues a mission and impact objectives.

Our mission is to promote the reuse of public data. This mission is broken down into objectives and impact indicators.

1. Improve the discoverability of open data
2. Promote the quality of open data
3. Encourage the reuse of open data

Rituals

In practice, it is the product owner's responsibility to synthesize needs and represent the user's voice within the team.
We work in two-week sprints, where we plan the tasks to be completed.

The goal is to assume deliberate prioritization by asking, what evolution of the application will bring the most value to the user at this moment? This also involves saying no regularly (or, at worst, "later") to protect the interests of both the user and the team, and ultimately to ensure that we remain aligned with the product vision.

We also strive to design features that are as "small" as possible.

The larger a feature or evolution is:

- the more likely we are to get stuck in an endless tunnel
- the more bugs we'll have to deal with
- the longer it will take to put into production, delaying value delivery to the user
- the longer it will take to get feedback on usage
- the higher the risk of having worked for nothing

We also aim to have the shortest feedback loop possible: changes are rolled out quickly because they are small and non-parallelized, tests are systematic, and usage and impact are measured. All of this helps us learn as quickly as possible whether the change effectively improves the product, and to gain more insight into user behavior, their expectations, etc., and ultimately to learn how to improve the product.

Among the activities undertaken to promote the platform, we can mention:

Our actions on social media, our blog, and our newsletter, which aim to promote activity on the platform and best practices in open data:

- Twitter (36k followers)
- LinkedIn (11k followers)
- Mastodon (2.2k followers)

column2:
Do you monitor what keywords are used to search for data and content on the portal?

For Explanation:
* If yes, please briefly (1) describe your process and (2) how you use the insights to improve the portal
column4: new question
column7:
We track the keywords searched using our traffic monitoring tool, Matomo.

However, this is not our main priority, as we have observed that the majority of users come from search engines like Google rather than our internal search engine. Tracking the most popular datasets is often more insightful for identifying trends.

On the other hand, we display a dedicated form when a search yields few or no results. This allows us to identify datasets that need to be opened or are poorly documented and therefore don't rank well in search results, based on user feedback.

We also occasionally monitor the use of filters.

Fun fact: one year, we identified the word "goat" as one of the most searched terms on the platform. After investigating, we discovered that a question in the national digital education program PIX, mandatory for middle school students, asked them to find the number of goats in a department using data.gouv.fr.

column2:
Do you monitor the most and least consulted pages?

For Explanation:
* If yes, please briefly (1) describe your process and (2) how you use the insights to improve the portal
* For informational purposes, kindly provide the URLs to the five most popular datasets on the portal
column4: new question
column7:
We closely monitor the most viewed pages and the most popular new content. For example, a top 10 list is displayed daily on the team's communication tool.

This allows us to identify trending topics to develop further (e.g., writing a dedicated article or highlighting specific datasets).

It also helps us determine when data exploration is relevant. For instance, some datasets are very popular because users are often looking for information rather than raw data. This insight helps us decide which datasets to redirect users to or when to create a dedicated data exploration.

For example, on the dataset of deaths, we display an information banner to redirect users who are looking for a specific death record rather than the entire database. In 2024, 38% of users who visited this dataset clicked on the link to the dedicated data exploration, allowing them to conduct a more specific search.

The five datasets that regularly appear in the top are:

- Fichier des personnes décédées (File of deceased persons)
- Demandes de valeurs foncières (Requests for property values)
- Répertoire national des associations (National directory of associations)
- Base SIRENE des entreprises et de leurs établissements (SIREN, SIRET)
- Liste publique des organismes de formation (L. 6351-7-1 of the Labor Code)

It's worth noting that some datasets may generate a lot of traffic but are strongly tied to current events (e.g., datasets on elections, fuel prices, or COVID-19 data).

We also monitor traffic on data reuses for the same reasons.

column2:
Do you take measures to optimise the search and discoverability of content (data and editorial)? 

For Explanation:
*If yes, please briefly describe how your optimise the search
column4:
We launch in 2021 a new search engine.
On top of that, the team is always working on the curation of the datasets on the portal and do their best to prevent inappropriate content (publicity mainly).

From the [platform's activity report](https://agarrone.github.io/public-files/moderation.pdf) which is sent to him every morning the data editor selects on a daily basis the most relevant datasets to highlight on the home page and on the different thematic pages. On top of that we work on the improvement of the search engine, for example:

- the tag system of the datasets makes it possible to optimize the search
- the "highlight" button for the platform administrator allows to bring up a data set in the ranking

We also carry out technical developments, which are based on log analysis:

[Keep track of udata search results performances](https://github.com/etalab/datagouv-search-indicator)

In order to highlight the key datasets published on the platform, we offer editorial content:

- We publish an [article every month](https://www.data.gouv.fr/fr/posts/suivi-des-sorties-mai-2020/) to showcase the most important publications (datasets or reuses) during the last month
- We offer the subscription to a [newsletter](https://infolettres.etalab.gouv.fr/subscribe/r1aq92xnj) .
- We publish articles on [Etalab's blog](https://www.etalab.gouv.fr/) in order to make some popular publications visible.
- Other articles about new data sets are posted [here](https://www.data.gouv.fr/fr/posts/)
- We highlight specific content on our [social network](https://twitter.com/datagouvfr)
- Users receive notifications when new data sets are available on the national portal (RSS, ATOM feeds, email notifications etc)

column2: 2.3 Data provision

column4:
All public sector providers contribute to the portal:

- The central administration: ministries and its operators
- The territorial administration: regions, department and cities

Examples:

- [Ministry](https://www.data.gouv.fr/fr/organizations/ministere-de-l-interieur/)
- [Operator](https://www.data.gouv.fr/fr/organizations/ademe/)
- [Region](https://www.data.gouv.fr/fr/organizations/region-ile-de-france/)
- [Department](https://www.data.gouv.fr/fr/organizations/departement-du-loiret/)
- [City](https://www.data.gouv.fr/fr/organizations/ville-d-issy-les-moulineaux/)****

Each public organization can contribute directly to the portal (by direct upload or by API) or publish their data on their own portal. When they do publish on their own portal, they have the possibility to be harvested by the national portal (data.gouv.fr). Each organization can ask support from the national portal team.

column4:
A strong focus has been put on dynamic data lately in particular on data regarding the epidemic which are automaticaly published every day. 

The best achievements on real time data have been achieved on [transport data](https://transport.data.gouv.fr/datasets?filter=has_realtime&type=public-transit#datasets-results).

The transport.data.gouv.fr task force deploys special efforts to promote real-time data. This includes [documentation](https://doc.transport.data.gouv.fr/producteurs/operateurs-de-transport-regulier-de-personnes/temps-reel-des-transports-en-commun) on standardisation, an [inventory of real time](https://transport.data.gouv.fr/real_time) data yet to be standardized, and [discussion with stakeholders](https://doc.transport.data.gouv.fr/documentation/liste-des-rencontres-publiques/20-09-2018-transport-regulier-temps-reel)

There are other examples such as [data on air quality](https://www.data.gouv.fr/fr/datasets/donnees-temps-reel-de-mesure-des-concentrations-de-polluants-atmospheriques-reglementes-1/) or [biodiversity data](https://www.data.gouv.fr/fr/datasets/description-des-especes-de-faune-et-flore-du-parc-national-des-ecrins/) or [tourism data](https://www.data.gouv.fr/fr/datasets/datatourisme-la-base-nationale-des-donnees-du-tourisme-en-open-data/) for instance.

column2:
Does this monitoring enable the portal team and/or data providers to take action to improve their performance on the national portal?

For Explanation:
* If yes, please (1) explain how and (2) if applicable provide the direct-URL to this feature.
column4:
Data publisher have several tools to monitor the main performance of their metadata or data features:

**Stats.data.gouv.fr**

Every publisher can monitor the number of visit of each dataset they have published [here](https://stats.data.gouv.fr/index.php?module=CoreHome&action=index&idSite=1&period=range&date=previous30#?idSite=1&period=range&date=previous30&category=General_Actions&subcategory=General_Pages)

**Quality of the metadata**

Any published dataset on the platform has a meta data quality checklist in their admin dashboard page. The questions are:

- Is the dataset described?
- Are keywords added?
- Is the format opened?
- Are discussions opened?
- Is the dataset up to date?
- Is the dataset available?

When a criterion is not met, a scheme indicates it to the producer.
